library(dlm)
#library(fpp2)

Introduction

Have a look at the dlm vignette.

dlm = dynamic linear model, basically a linear Gaussian state-space model. Dynamic refers to the property that the state will change over time.

Random Walk plus Noise

To simulate values from a random walk plus noise model, V, W, m0 and C0 are needed.

rwpn <- function(V = 0.8, W = 0.2, m0 = 0, C0 = 100, n = 100) {
 
  y <- numeric(n)
  mu <- numeric(n)
  
  for (i in 1:n) {
    if (i == 1) mu[i] <- rnorm(1, m0, C0)
    else mu[i] <- rnorm(1, mu[i-1], W)
    y[i] <- rnorm(1, mu[i], V)
  }
  
  return(y)
}

y <- rwpn()

plot.ts(y)

Define dlm model

For now we assume that the parameters are known. We have observations and want to estimate the state, and perhaps also predict future observations.

Start by defining the model. Here we define a random walk plus noise state-space model, through the matrices F and G. We also specify the parameters and the mean and variance of the prior (initial state) m0 and C0.

## define model
mod.rwpn <- dlm(FF = 1, V = 0.8, GG = 1, W = 0.2, m0 = 0, C0 = 100)

An alternative, equivalent way to define this model is by using dlmModPoly

dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = 0.8, dW = 0.2, C0 = 100)
$FF
     [,1]
[1,]    1

$V
     [,1]
[1,]  0.8

$GG
     [,1]
[1,]    1

$W
     [,1]
[1,]  0.2

$m0
[1] 0

$C0
     [,1]
[1,]  100

Careful with the defaults of the above arguments. dV and dW refer to the diagonal elements of the V and W matrices.

order = 1 means that the state follows a random walk. order = 2 (second order polynomial) refers to a random walk plus drift model for the state. This terminology comes from the fact that if you would take 1st or 2nd order differences of the observations you would end up with a stationary process (tut question).

We have now defined the structure of the model, with all the familiar state space model matrices:

mod.rwpn
$FF
     [,1]
[1,]    1

$V
     [,1]
[1,]  0.8

$GG
     [,1]
[1,]    1

$W
     [,1]
[1,]  0.2

$m0
[1] 0

$C0
     [,1]
[1,]  100

We could also change these matrices individually (useful for more complicated models). For example:

C0(mod.rwpn)
     [,1]
[1,]  100
C0(mod.rwpn) <- 80
C0(mod.rwpn)
     [,1]
[1,]   80

Kalman Filter

The Kalman filter is used to estimate the state, and to make predictions of future states. The dlmFilter function needs the data and the model.

filt1 <- dlmFilter(y, mod.rwpn)
names(filt1)
[1] "y"   "mod" "m"   "U.C" "D.C" "a"   "U.R" "D.R" "f"

dlmFilter will return the states (m), and various variance matrices.

D.C together with U.C gives the SVD of the variances of the estimation errors. The variance of \(m_t - \theta_t\) is given by U.C[[t]] %*% diag(D.C[t,]^2) %*% t(U.C[[t]]).

\(\theta_t | y_{1:t} \sim N(m_t C_t)\)

D.R together with U.R gives the SVD of the variances of the prediction errors. The variance of \(a_t - \theta_t\) is given by U.R[[t]] %*% diag(D.R[t,]^2) %*% t(U.R[[t]]).

\(\theta_t | y_{1:t-1} \sim N(a_t R_t)\)

Note that the estimated state vector m is longer than the original time series:

plot.ts(y, las = 1)

Maximum Likelihood

What if we did not know the parameter values (V, W)? Which is probably the reality most of the time.

The Kalman Filter can also be used to set up the likelihood, and then we can maximise this likelihood. This can be done using dlmMLE(), which sends the likelihood function to optim(). First we need to define the likelihood function. We also use the model definition functions for this, except that we substitute unknown parameter values for the variances. The first argument of the likelihood function must be the parameter vector. parm contains estimates for starting values for the parameters.

Both V and W need to be positive, therefore use exp(parm). This is a common trick used to obtain appropriate MLEs.

# define the likelihood function
lik.fun <- function(x) {
 dlmModPoly(1, dV = exp(x[1]), dW = exp(x[2]))
}

# maximize the likelihood
fit <- dlmMLE(y, parm = c(0,0), build = lik.fun)

fit$conv
[1] 0
fit
$par
[1] -0.4052241 -3.3573364

$value
[1] 49.29081

$counts
function gradient 
      11       11 

$convergence
[1] 0

$message
[1] "CONVERGENCE: REL_REDUCTION_OF_F <= FACTR*EPSMCH"

The object returned from dlmMLE is what is returned by optim. A code of 0 for convergence means success.

The variances (V and W) are estimated as

exp(fit$par)
[1] 0.6668274 0.0348279

The true values were 0.8 and 0.2.

Forecasting

Before you run the following code, or look at the output, predict what the forecasts will look like (we have fitted a random walk plus noise model).

model.fit <- lik.fun(fit$par)
model.filtered <- dlmFilter(y, model.fit)

model.forecast <- dlmForecast(model.filtered, nAhead = 10)

Local linear model

This can be set up as above or by just using dlmModPoly, whose default is the local linear model (order = 2).

myMod <- dlmModPoly()

Up to you: repeat the above on the local linear model.

What happens with missing observaions?

Seasonality - Basic Structural Model

We are going to fit the basic structural model to the monthly CO\(_2\) data co2. This will have 12 seasonal effects.

\[ \begin{align*} Y_t &= \mu_t + s_t + v_t, \qquad & v_t \sim N(0, V) \\ \mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_t, & w_t \sim N(0, \sigma_w^2) \\ \beta_t &= \beta_{t-1} + \gamma_t, & \gamma_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\gamma})\\ \\ s_t &= - \sum_{j=1}^{S-1} s_{t-j} + \delta_t, & \delta_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\delta}) \\ \end{align*} \]

plot(co2, las = 1)

We can use dlmModSeas to add these seasonal effects \(s_{it}\).

m.s1 <-  dlmModPoly() + dlmModSeas(12)
m.s1$W

Note: It seems that the default is to set \(\sigma_w^2 = 0\) (first diagonal element of \(W\)).

Define the likelihood function

We need to estimate the parameters (four variance parameters). The exp(p[i]) trick is used to ensure the variance estimates are positive.

lik.s1 <- function(p) {
  mod <- dlmModPoly() + dlmModSeas(12)
  
  W(mod)[1, 1] <- exp(p[1])
  W(mod)[2, 2] <- exp(p[2])
  W(mod)[3, 3] <- exp(p[3])
  
  V(mod) <- exp(p[4])
  
  return(mod)
}

Seasonality with trigonometric terms

An alternative way to add seasonality to state-space models is through cos and sin terms, like in a harmonic regression model.

\[\begin{align*} Y_t &= \mu_t + g_t + v_t, \qquad & v_t \sim N(0, V) \\ \mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_t, & w_t \sim N(0, \sigma_w^2) \\ \beta_t &= \beta_{t-1} + \gamma_t, & \gamma_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\gamma})\\ \end{align*}\]

where

\(g_t = a cos(t \omega) + b sin(t \omega)\)

and \(\omega\) is the frequency (in radians): \(\omega = \frac{2 \pi }{s}\). \(s\) is the period (length of a full cycle in terms of number of observations). This adds a sinusoidal curve to the seasona effects.

More generally, we define the Fourier frequencies as

\[\omega_j = \frac{2 \pi j}{s}\]

\(s\) is the period (length of a full cycle in terms of number of observations). For \(j=1\) a full cycle (\(2 \pi\)) is completed in \(s\) time steps. For \(j = 2\), two full cycles are completed in \(s\) time steps (\(4 \pi\)).

To add more flexible seasonal patterns we could add terms with higher frequencies, \(j = 0, 1, ..., \frac{s}{2}\),

Define the jth harmonic as

\[S_j(t) = a_j cos(t \omega_j) + b_j sin(t \omega_j)\]

and \(g_t = \sum a_j cos(t \omega_j) + b_j sin(t \omega_j)\)

The updating equation is a bit more complicated and needs the conjugate harmonic

\[S^*_j(t) = - a_j sin(t \omega_j) + b_j sin(t \omega_j)\]

In dlm, to add such harmonic terms to the state-space model we can use the function dlmModTrig:

## first check if this is the structure we want
m.s1 <-  dlmModPoly() + dlmModTrig(s = 12, q = 1)
m.s1
$FF
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    0    1    0

$V
     [,1]
[1,]    2

$GG
     [,1] [,2]       [,3]      [,4]
[1,]    1    1  0.0000000 0.0000000
[2,]    0    1  0.0000000 0.0000000
[3,]    0    0  0.8660254 0.5000000
[4,]    0    0 -0.5000000 0.8660254

$W
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    0    0    0    0
[2,]    0    1    0    0
[3,]    0    0    0    0
[4,]    0    0    0    0

$m0
[1] 0 0 0 0

$C0
      [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]
[1,] 1e+07 0e+00 0e+00 0e+00
[2,] 0e+00 1e+07 0e+00 0e+00
[3,] 0e+00 0e+00 1e+07 0e+00
[4,] 0e+00 0e+00 0e+00 1e+07

\(s\) is called period in this function, q is the number of harmonics to include.

period = time it takes to complete one cycle

frequency = number of cycles per unit time: \(f = 1 / P\)

Fit such a model to the CO\(_2\) data and compare with the previous model. Do you need more than one harmonic?
